section_summary: This section documents the severe deterioration of Japanese agriculture during the Depression, emphasizing collapsing crop and silk prices, heavy rural indebtedness, tenant-landlord relations, and the potential for agrarian and military-linked unrest. Embassy despatches and translated newspaper articles examine proposed relief programs and the agrarian legislation enacted in 1933, while later records address foreign participation in natural-resource development and agriculture. The section concludes with a 1938 private letter proposing hydroponics as a possible response to Japan’s food and land problems and as an inducement to end the war in China.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Relief for Farmers
subfiles.about: The note directs the reader to report No. 219 concerning plans for financial relief of Japan’s farming population.
subfiles.summary: This filing sheet identifies an attached account of a late-July meeting in Tokyo of chairmen of local agricultural bodies. The meeting considered financial relief for farmers and produced proposals for submission to government agencies.

subfiles.title: Relief for Farmers
subfiles.about: The report summarizes a Tokyo meeting convened to formulate financial-relief plans for Japanese farmers.
subfiles.summary: Representatives discussed reducing senior officials’ salaries, revising pensions, lowering educational expenditures, creating employment through road and land improvements, and reducing farm-village debts. A committee prepared concrete proposals, and resolutions were submitted to government agencies. The ministers responsible for home affairs and agriculture and forestry reportedly promised assistance.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 473 Transmitting a Report on Agriculture and Social Unrest
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forbes transmits an enclosed report on Japanese agriculture and social unrest in rural districts.
subfiles.summary: The brief covering despatch calls the Department’s attention to the agricultural situation in Japan and unrest in the countryside. Its sole enclosure is the detailed report that follows.

subfiles.title: Agriculture and Social Unrest in Japan
subfiles.about: The report analyzes Japan’s agricultural depression and assesses whether rural distress could produce organized or sporadic violence.
subfiles.summary: The report documents sharp declines in the value of rice, cocoons, tea, wheat, barley, and other crops while farmers’ costs, taxes, and debts remained disproportionately high. It examines the circumstances of landlords, owner-farmers, tenants, and agricultural laborers, as well as tenant unions, landlord unions, disputes, and “harmonization” organizations. Rural communities are described as having reached a financial impasse, although weak organization, police pressure, conservatism, and loyalty to the Emperor made coordinated revolt seem unlikely. The Embassy nevertheless considered sporadic violence possible and warned that broader disturbances could draw farmers into more unified action.

subfiles.title: Departmental Summary of Tokyo Despatch No. 19
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes a despatch on farmers’ distress, military involvement, and proposed government relief.
subfiles.summary: The summary estimates farmers’ debts at six billion yen and notes that nearly half the population depended on agriculture, with northern farmers described as destitute. It stresses that the agrarian problem became a major political issue after reports connected the super-patriotic military with rural agitation. The Diet called for an extraordinary session to consider relief measures.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 19: Plight of the Farmers in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reviews the worsening agrarian crisis, its political implications, and competing proposals for farm relief.
subfiles.summary: The despatch describes destitution in northern prefectures caused by poor rice crops, the raw-silk collapse, unemployment, taxation, and high-interest debt. It links heightened public concern to the May 15 violence, the rural origins of many soldiers, and indications of military participation in agrarian agitation. Farmers’ associations demanded a debt moratorium, fertilizer aid, and assistance for emigration to Manchuria, while the Minseitō and Seiyūkai advanced rival relief programs. The Diet ultimately requested another extraordinary session, and the Home Ministry considered a large public-works program.

subfiles.title: The Relief of Farming Communities and Manufacturers
subfiles.about: The editorial considers the fiscal and inflationary consequences of large-scale relief for farmers and small businesses.
subfiles.summary: The editorial argues that farm and commercial debts had grown so large that government aid was unavoidable but could endanger state finances. It distinguishes the government’s fiscal responsibility from the political parties’ freedom to make popular promises. The writer anticipates inflation and questions how another extraordinary Diet session could finance genuinely effective relief.

subfiles.title: Debts of Farmers
subfiles.about: The article presents national and local evidence of farmers’ crushing debts and operating losses.
subfiles.summary: The article attributes rural insolvency to falling agricultural prices, expensive fertilizer, unchanged taxes, and loans secured against cocoons and growing rice. Data from Fukushima and Hyogo prefectures illustrate heavy personal and public debt and annual deficits among rice farmers and sericulturists. It reviews proposals for low-interest refinancing, government bonds, tax reductions, debt adjustment, and public works. Comparative figures for 1919 and 1931 show a formerly profitable rice farm operating at a loss.

subfiles.title: Document File Note for Despatch No. 38
subfiles.about: The note points to a periodic report discussing Japan’s increasingly serious agricultural situation.
subfiles.summary: The filing sheet records that the Cabinet decided to summon another extraordinary Diet session to confront the farm crisis. It highlights demands for a three-year debt moratorium and state assistance with fertilizer purchases.

subfiles.title: Immigration and Labor Matters: Agricultural Distress
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: This extract reports extreme distress in farming communities and the growing political activity of farmers’ organizations.
subfiles.summary: The report says northern farmers were destitute and had little prospect of paying debts or taxes. Government attention had increased partly because of military interest in the issue and the rural origins of soldiers. Farmers’ representatives sought a three-year debt moratorium and public assistance for fertilizer purchases.

subfiles.title: Document File Note for Harbin Despatch No. 5463
subfiles.about: The note refers to a report alleging preparations for an agrarian revolution in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This filing sheet cross-references a Harbin despatch concerning reports of agrarian revolutionary activity in Japan. The reported movement was attributed to the acute crisis affecting the rural population.

subfiles.title: Agrarian Revolution in Japan
subfiles.about: The extract discusses and disputes information that Japanese farmers were preparing an open revolution.
subfiles.summary: A German consular source had reportedly received information that agrarian groups in Japan were preparing a revolution because of the rural crisis. The report rejects or qualifies the information attributed to Dr. Kaiser and indicates that the major political parties were concerned with the welfare of the farming population. Much of the page is damaged by poor OCR, so its finer distinctions are uncertain.

subfiles.title: Departmental Summary of Tokyo Despatch No. 390
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes three recently enacted Japanese agrarian laws and the Embassy’s assessment of them.
subfiles.summary: The Rice and Other Cereals Control Law sought to regulate supply and prices, while the Agrarian Debt Adjustment Association Law created debt-adjustment guilds and a two-hundred-million-yen loan fund. The Agricultural Property Credit Law allowed farmers and fishermen to mortgage movable occupational property. The Embassy regarded the debt fund as inadequate and warned that easier credit might merely increase rural indebtedness.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 390: Agrarian Legislation
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew evaluates three laws intended to address Japan’s persistent agricultural and rural-credit problems.
subfiles.summary: The despatch argues that inflation and competing news had reduced public attention to rural distress without resolving it. It details the new law for government control of rice and other cereals, the creation of agrarian debt-adjustment guilds, and the authorization of mortgages on movable agricultural and fishing property. Grew considers the debt-adjustment funding wholly insufficient compared with six billion yen in rural debts. He also warns that the new property-credit system, though useful for obtaining capital, could deepen farmers’ debt burdens.

subfiles.title: Document File Note for Despatch No. 419
subfiles.about: The note points to a report stating that conditions in Japan’s agricultural districts remained as bad as during the previous year.
subfiles.summary: The filing sheet identifies a periodic despatch on continuing agricultural distress. It emphasizes that reduced press attention did not signify a meaningful improvement in rural conditions.

subfiles.title: General Economic and Financial Conditions: Agrarian Problems
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The extract reviews persistent farm distress and summarizes the government’s three principal agrarian laws.
subfiles.summary: Rural debts were still increasing, while the cost of farmers’ necessities rose faster than farm-product prices. The report summarizes the Rice Control Law, the Agrarian Debt Adjustment Association Law, and the Agricultural Property Credit Law. It concludes that these measures were inadequate in relation to the scale of farmers’ debts.

subfiles.title: Document File Note for Telegram No. 68
subfiles.about: The note identifies a telegram on legal and administrative restrictions affecting foreign exploitation of Japanese natural resources and agriculture.
subfiles.summary: This filing sheet points to Telegram No. 68 concerning foreign access to mining, water power, fishing, agriculture, and labor. A copy of the telegram is attached on the following pages.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 68: Foreign Exploitation of Natural Resources and Agriculture
subfiles.about: The telegram explains the legal and administrative position of foreigners seeking to exploit natural resources or conduct farming in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Apart from mining law and nationality restrictions on subsidies, Japan had few explicit statutory barriers to foreign resource development. Administrative practice would probably prevent foreigners from receiving water-power or commercial-fishing concessions, though foreign investment could occur through Japanese concession holders. Agriculture itself was unrestricted, and foreign missionary institutions operated farms without interference. Importing foreign labor would probably be blocked through Home Department and police immigration rulings that were not subject to habeas corpus review.

subfiles.title: Letter Proposing Hydroponics for Japan
subfiles.about: Nanish urges Hull to consider hydroponics as a response to Japan’s agricultural predicament and war in China.
subfiles.summary: The writer encloses or references a Saturday Evening Post article on “liquid farming,” or hydroponics, which promised large and varied crops on small areas. He suggests that the method could suit land-scarce Japan and that chemicals used for munitions might instead produce food and industrial crops. He hopes American persuasion and propaganda could use the idea to encourage Japan to end the war in China and asks that the letter not receive an official acknowledgment.
